correctness.rationale: Under the stated convention a position swap acts on the right, so balls are gT for the identity plus five involutions. They each have six words, forcing twenty centers. The six right translates Ht are disjoint: the difference of generators is a transposition with three fixed symbols, a three-cycle, or a disjoint pair of cycle-edge transpositions. The first two cannot belong to the affine group (fixed points and order); an affine involution x↦−x+b pairing consecutive residues on two distinct edges would require their sums, hence their starting indices, to agree. Thus H is perfect, and all left cosets are perfect by relabeling values. The supplied Python and C++ exact covers search all compatible balls covering a chosen uncovered word after starting at the identity, which is legitimate by relabeling. Their first-singleton shortcut may postpone finding a zero-candidate word, without changing completeness; it does not always choose a global minimum as informally stated. An independent unrestricted implementation chooses the lexicographically first uncovered word, enumerates all possible disjoint balls through it without requiring identity or affine structure, and returns exactly the six left cosets (1937 nodes and 696 dead ends). The last phrase 'no nonaffine perfect code' is understood in context as no inequivalent design outside those cosets, not as saying every labeled codeword is literally affine in the fixed coordinates.

value.rationale: This classifies all perfect designs for the cyclic channel at the length of its canonical affine example. The result determines the exact design freedom (one isometry orbit, six labeled codebooks) rather than just improving a bound or exhibiting another example. It is a useful small exact benchmark for rigid perfect codes in permutation Cayley graphs.
residual_risks: It does not generalize to arbitrary lengths or error radii.
